title: Processes
summary: See running programs, run them in the background and stop them: ps, &, $!, kill, jobs.
intro:
Every program that runs on your computer is a process.
Right now there are hundreds of them: your browser, your music, this app...
In this lesson you will look at processes, start one in the background, find it and stop it.
One note: in Terminal Academy, every command line runs in a fresh shell. So jobs only knows jobs from the same line. Your real terminal remembers more.
outro: You can now see, start and stop processes like a real system admin! Remember: & sends a program to the background, $! gives you its PID, and kill stops it.

steps.instruction: Show the processes that are running in your terminal.
steps.explain: Every running program gets a number: the PID (process ID). The CMD column shows the name of the program. You may even see ps itself in the list!

steps.instruction: Run the script ./slow.sh and wait until it finishes.
steps.explain: That was a foreground process: the terminal waits until it ends, and you can't type anything else. If a program takes too long, Ctrl+C stops it.

steps.instruction: Now start sleep 300 in the background. In the same line, save its PID in the file sleep.pid.
hints: Put & after a command to run it in the background. Then $! holds the PID of that background process.
echo $! > sleep.pid writes the PID into a file.
steps.explain: sleep 300 waits 300 seconds and does nothing else. Thanks to & you got your prompt back at once: the process runs in the background. Type cat sleep.pid to see its PID.

steps.instruction: Find the sleep process in the list of ALL processes.
hints: ps aux shows all processes. That's a lot, so send the list to grep with a pipe |.
steps.explain: The second column is the PID. It's the same number as in sleep.pid. You may also see the grep command itself in the list, because it was running too!

steps.instruction: Stop the sleep process with kill and its PID.
hints: kill PID, for example: kill 12345 (use YOUR number, from cat sleep.pid or from step 4).
You can also let the shell read the number for you: $(cat sleep.pid)
steps.explain: kill sends a signal that asks a process to stop. kill -9 PID forces it, but use that only when a normal kill does not work. Check with ps aux | grep sleep: the sleep 300 is gone.

steps.instruction: In ONE line, start sleep 5 in the background and then list your jobs.
hints: First the background command with &, then the command jobs. Both on the same line.
steps.explain: jobs lists the background jobs of your shell. In a real terminal you can also type fg to bring a job back to the foreground, or kill %1 to stop job number 1.
